title: Pick the right shape
scenario: Your team has four automation ideas on the board and one budget line. Before choosing tools, you need to stop the agent-shaped answer from being applied to workflow-shaped problems.
task: Pick the idea that genuinely needs an agent — a system that decides its own steps — rather than a fixed workflow or a single prompt.

options.text: Enter three fixed fields from every incoming invoice into the ledger
options.feedback: The path is known and the output is checkable: a workflow, run at volume, with exception handling for the odd invoice. No loop decisions needed.

options.text: Triage 300 support tickets a day into five queues defined by written rules
options.feedback: Fixed rules, fixed queues — a workflow. It will be cheaper, and its mistakes will be findable by auditing the rules.

options.text: Find out why cancellations rose in one region last month, drawing on reports, survey text and support notes
options.feedback: The next step depends on what the previous one found — that is the agent signature. Bound it with a question, a budget and a human review, and it earns its loop.

options.text: Convert a folder of 80 scanned forms into spreadsheet rows
options.feedback: Repetitive, known steps, verifiable output — workflow. If a page fails, route it to a human queue; no step-by-step decisions required.

hints: Ask whether the path is known in advance. Known path → workflow; unknown path that reacts to findings → maybe agent.
If you could write the steps down as a checklist before starting, an agent is usually a more expensive checklist.
explanation: Three of the four ideas have a written path: extract, classify, convert — repetitive steps with checkable outputs. Those are workflows, and they should stay that way. The churn investigation is different: the useful next move depends on the last result, so the sequence cannot be authored in advance. That is when an agent loop can pay — provided it is bounded by a clear question, a budget and a review gate at the end.
